front: Walk through what happens between g++ main.cpp pricing.cpp -o app and a running executable. Where does the linker come in, and is anything interpreted at runtime?
back:
Answer: Each .cpp file is a separate translation unit, processed on its own, and the linker joins their object files into one native executable. Nothing is interpreted: the executable is native machine code.
Why: (1) The preprocessor expands #include (it pastes the header text in) and #define macros. (2) The compiler turns that text into machine code and writes an object file (.o) holding the functions it defines, plus a list of symbols it needs from elsewhere. (3) The linker joins all object files and libraries, resolves every needed symbol against a definition in another object, and writes one executable.
Python contrast: import runs a module at runtime and binds names in a namespace dict. In C++ every name is resolved at build time, so a missing function is a link error, not a NameError at call time.
Interview trap: A header is not a compilation unit. Every .cpp that includes it gets its own copy of the text, so a definition placed in a header can be duplicated across objects.
Build pipeline: each .cpp becomes an object file, then the linker joins them into one native executable.

Answer: The header is the interface: it gives main.cpp the signature so the call type-checks. The .cpp file holds the single definition. The linker matches the call in main.cpp to the definition in pricing.cpp by the symbol for pv(double, double).
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
95
Interview trap: The include guard (#ifndef PRICING_H) stops a second inclusion inside one translation unit. It does not stop two different .cpp files from each defining the same function (see the multiple-definition card).

Answer: The declaration satisfies the compiler, but nothing supplies a definition, so the linker cannot resolve the symbol.
Output (g++ diagnostics):
main.cpp:(.text.startup+0x29): undefined reference to `pv(double, double)'
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
Fix: define pv in a .cpp file that is passed to the link step, or define it in the same file. A declaration alone is a promise the linker checks.
Interview trap: The error comes from the linker, not the compiler, which is why it can appear only after a successful compile of every file.

front:
dup.h defines int lot_size() without inline, and both a.cpp and main.cpp include it. What is the build result, and what is the standard fix?
dup.h
#ifndef DUP_H
#define DUP_H

int lot_size() { return 1000000; }   // definition in a header, no inline

#endif
a.cpp
#include "dup.h"

int a_lots() { return lot_size() / 1000; }
main.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include "dup.h"

int a_lots();

int main() {
    std::cout << a_lots() << ' ' << lot_size() << '\n';
}
back:
Answer: Each .cpp gets its own definition of lot_size. The linker sees two strong definitions of one symbol and fails.
Output (g++ diagnostics):
main.cpp:(.text+0x0): multiple definition of `lot_size()'; /tmp/ccdhgypI.o:a.cpp:(.text+0x0): first defined here
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
Fix: mark it inline, which lets identical definitions appear in several translation units (the One Definition Rule still applies, so every copy must be identical).
Output with the fix:
1000 1000000
Alternative: put the definition in one .cpp and keep only the declaration in the header. constexpr functions are implicitly inline. Function templates may also be defined in a header, because the One Definition Rule allows identical template definitions in several translation units; this is how header-only libraries work.
Interview trap: An include guard does not help here. It only prevents a second inclusion within one translation unit.

front: Each .cpp file is one {{c1::translation unit}}. #include is textual, so the header text is {{c2::pasted in}} before compilation, and the linker sees only {{c3::object-file symbols}}.
back: The compiler checks types within each translation unit separately. Cross-file consistency is only checked by the programmer, or by the linker through symbol names.

Answer: long is 8 bytes on this 64-bit Linux build, but the standard does not guarantee that width.
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
char        1
int         4
long        8
long long   8
double      8
void*       8
int64_t     8
Why: The sizes are not guaranteed by the standard.
Trap: long is 8 bytes on 64-bit Linux (LP64) but 4 bytes on 64-bit Windows (LLP64). Code that assumes its width breaks across platforms. Use std::int64_t from <cstdint> when the width matters.

front: The standard guarantees that int is at least {{c1::16}} bits, long at least {{c2::32}} bits and long long at least {{c3::64}} bits. For an exact width, use {{c4::std::int64_t}} from <cstdint>.
back: Minimum widths are guarantees from the standard, not sizes. On GCC with LP64 you see int = 4, long = 8, long long = 8 bytes, as in the sizes card.

Answer: Signed integer overflow is undefined behaviour in C++, so the optimiser may fold x + 1 > x to true for every x.
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
true
true
Why: The optimiser may assume x + 1 never overflows. Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2N, so the same test on unsigned is a real comparison.
GCC 13 also prints true for always_true(INT_MAX) at -O0, so the fold happens even without optimisation (the x86 codegen at -O0 is a constant mov $1). With -fwrapv, which defines signed overflow as wraparound, the same program prints true then false, the answer a wrapping reading would give.
Interview trap: "It wraps around on my machine" is not a safe mental model: the compiler may assume no overflow happens. For notional times price products, use std::int64_t with range checks, or double where the quantity is an estimate.

Answer: Since C++11, integer division truncates toward zero, and the sign of a % b follows the dividend a.
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
-3 -1 -3 1
Why: Python floors the quotient and gives the sign of the divisor for %: -4 1 -4 -1.
Interview trap: a / b with two int operands never returns a fraction. The result is cast only after the truncation.

front: Implement int floor_div(int a, int b) for b > 0 that matches Python's a // b for negative a. Show the code and its test output.
back:
Answer: Take C++'s truncated quotient, then step down by one when the division was inexact and the true quotient is negative.
Code
#include <cassert>
#include <iostream>

// floor division for b > 0, matching Python's a // b
int floor_div(int a, int b) {
    int q = a / b;                       // truncates toward zero
    if (a % b != 0 && a < 0) --q;        // step down when the true quotient is negative
    return q;
}

int main() {
    std::cout << floor_div(-7, 2) << ' ' << floor_div(7, 2) << ' '
              << floor_div(-8, 2) << ' ' << floor_div(-1, 2) << '\n';
    assert(floor_div(-7, 2) == -4);
}
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
-4 3 -4 -1
Interview trap: The rule above is correct only for b > 0. For b < 0, Python floors with the sign of the divisor, so the test on a < 0 is wrong. Also, INT_MIN / -1 overflows and is undefined behaviour.

front: Since C++11, integer division truncates toward {{c1::zero}}, and the sign of a % b follows {{c2::the dividend a}}. So -7 / 2 evaluates to {{c3::-3}}.
back: Python's // floors instead, so -7 // 2 is -4. Porting quant code from Python needs explicit floor logic.

Answer: The int operand is converted to unsigned int for the comparison. -1 becomes 4294967295, so i < u is false.
g++ diagnostics:
main.cpp:6:11: warning: comparison of integer expressions of different signedness: ‘int’ and ‘unsigned int’ [-Wsign-compare]
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
i is not smaller
Interview trap: The same bug hides in loops such as for (int i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i). size() returns the unsigned std::size_t, and -Wsign-compare flags the mismatch. Use std::size_t for the index or compare with a checked cast.

Answer: IEEE 754 binary64 cannot represent 0.1 or 0.3 exactly. The sum rounds to a double one unit in the last place above the double nearest to 0.3, so == is false.
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
0.30000000000000004
false
Rule: never compare floating-point results with == unless they are exact by construction, such as small integers stored as doubles.
Interview trap: Floating-point addition is not associative. Reordering a sum over a portfolio changes the last digits of the result.

front: Implement approx_equal(a, b, rel_tol, abs_tol) that works both near zero and at large magnitudes. Why do you need the absolute tolerance?
back:
Answer: Accept when the difference is within either tolerance: |a - b| <= max(abs_tol, rel_tol * max(|a|, |b|)).
Code
#include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>

// |a - b| <= max(abs_tol, rel_tol * max(|a|, |b|))
bool approx_equal(double a, double b, double rel_tol = 1e-12, double abs_tol = 1e-14) {
    double diff = std::fabs(a - b);
    return diff <= std::max(abs_tol, rel_tol * std::max(std::fabs(a), std::fabs(b)));
}

int main() {
    std::cout << std::boolalpha;
    std::cout << approx_equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3) << '\n';
    std::cout << approx_equal(1.0, 1.0 + 1e-9) << '\n';
    std::cout << approx_equal(0.0, 1e-15) << '\n';
    std::cout << approx_equal(1e6, 1e6 + 1e-3) << '\n';
}
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
true
false
true
false
Why: The relative term alone vanishes at zero, so comparing 0.0 with 1e-15 would fail. The absolute term handles that case. The default rel_tol = 1e-12 is about 4,500 units of machine spacing at 1.0 (checked: 1e-12 / 2.22e-16 = 4503.6).
Interview trap: No single tolerance fits all quantities. A rate in decimals, a price in currency units and a PV01 need tolerances chosen for their scale.

Answer: 1.0 + 1e-16 rounds back to 1.0, because the spacing of doubles at 1.0 is 2.22e-16. So (1 + x) - 1 returns 0, not 1e-16. The same loss happens in any finite difference where the bump is tiny compared with the value being bumped.
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
0
true
Derivation: for a central difference (f(x+h) - f(x-h)) / 2h, truncation error scales as h^2 and rounding error as eps / h. Balancing them gives h of order eps^(1/3) times the scale of x, roughly 6e-6 relative (approx.).
Interview trap: Smaller bumps are not automatically more accurate. Below the optimum, rounding noise dominates.

front: A double has a {{c1::53}}-bit significand, so the spacing between adjacent doubles at 1.0 is {{c2::2-52}} (about {{c3::2.22e-16}}). This is exposed as std::numeric_limits<double>::epsilon().
back:
The spacing doubles at each power of two above 1 and halves below it. So the relative spacing is between about 1.1e-16 and 2.2e-16 across the range, not a fixed absolute tolerance.
IEEE 754 binary64 layout of 1.0, and the gap to the next double, which doubles at each power of two.

Answer: int a = 3.9; is copy-initialisation and compiles, silently truncating to 3. int b{3.9}; is list-initialisation, which forbids narrowing conversions, so it is an error.
g++ diagnostics:
main.cpp:5:11: error: narrowing conversion of ‘3.8999999999999999e+0’ from ‘double’ to ‘int’ [-Wnarrowing]
    5 |     int b{3.9};      // list-initialisation forbids narrowing: error
Interview trap: Braces catch narrowing only in initialisation. An = assignment or a function argument truncates silently.

Answer: Both operands are int, so the division is an integer division. It truncates before the result converts to double.
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
3 3.5
Why: static_cast<double>(notional) / lots converts one operand first, so the usual arithmetic conversions make the division floating-point. static_cast is the explicit C++ conversion that the compiler checks; prefer it to C-style casts like (double)x, which can silently do more.
Interview trap: double(notional / lots) is the common bug. The conversion happens after the division, so it still gives 3.

Answer: A reference is an alias for an existing object. It must be bound at declaration, it can't be null, and it can't be re-bound to another object. A pointer is a separate variable holding an address. It can be null, re-pointed and dereferenced.
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
42
7 42
Python contrast: r = x binds a second name to the same object, which is like a reference. r = 5 rebinds the name to a new int object and leaves x alone. In C++, r = 42 assigns through the alias into x.
Interview trap: int& r; without an initialiser is ill-formed. A reference has no null state to test for.
A reference is a second name for x; a pointer holds an address and can be re-pointed.

Answer: const int* p is a pointer to a const int. You may re-point p, but you may not write through it.
g++ diagnostics:
main.cpp:4:8: error: assignment of read-only location ‘* p’
Reading declarations: read from the name outwards. const int* p: pointer to const int. int* const p: const pointer to int, so p can't move but *p can change. const int* const p: neither.
Interview trap: const binds to the type immediately on its left, or on its right when nothing is on the left.

front: A {{c1::const}} variable cannot be modified through its name, but its initialiser may be a runtime value. A {{c2::constexpr}} variable must be initialised by a {{c3::constant expression}}, so its value is known at compile time.
back: Use constexpr for true compile-time constants such as a day-count convention or a basis-point scale. Marking a function constexpr allows compile-time evaluation but does not force it: the function can still run at runtime.

Answer: static_assert fails the build when its condition is false. Both discount_factor calls are constant expressions, so the checks run during compilation. 1 / (1 + 1) is exact in binary, so the == check is safe.
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
0.5
Interview trap: Do not static_assert equality on an inexact floating-point result. The check would depend on rounding.

Answer: f(2L) is ambiguous: it needs a conversion either way, and both candidates rank equally.
Why: f(2) matches f(int) exactly, and f(2.0) matches f(double) exactly. long to int is an integral conversion, and long to double is a conversion between integer and floating types. Both have the same rank, so the call fails.
g++ diagnostics:
main.cpp:9:6: error: call of overloaded ‘f(long int)’ is ambiguous
main.cpp:3:6: note: candidate: ‘void f(int)’
main.cpp:4:6: note: candidate: ‘void f(double)’
Fix: add an f(long) overload, or cast the argument at the call site.
Interview trap: Overload resolution ranks implicit conversions. It does not pick the most natural overload, and the return type plays no part in choosing.

Answer: Passing t by value to by_value copy-constructs a new Trade, so the counter goes to 1. const Trade& binds to the existing object and copies nothing.
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
copies: 1
Rule of thumb: pass scalars by value, and pass anything owning heap memory (vectors, strings) by const& for reading or by & for modifying.
Interview trap: A Python reader expects a mutable argument to be shared with the caller. In C++ a by-value parameter is a separate object, so changes made inside the function never reach the caller.

Answer: Names live in namespaces, and a qualified call such as rates::to_decimal picks one. Two functions with the same name in different namespaces do not clash.
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
0.0025 0.03
Interview trap: Never write using namespace std; (or any using-directive) in a header. It puts the names into every file that includes the header.

Answer: break is needed to stop fall-through. Here case 1 prints and then runs into case 2, so both strings print.
g++ diagnostics:
main.cpp:6:30: warning: this statement may fall through [-Wimplicit-fallthrough=]
main.cpp:7:9: note: here
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
short medium
Why: -Wimplicit-fallthrough (in -Wextra) warns about this. Mark deliberate fall-through with [[fallthrough]]; (C++17).
Interview trap: Unlike Python's match, a C++ case label has no implicit break. Forgetting it is one of the most common silent bugs.

Answer: std::string owns its characters and has value semantics. += appends, and == compares contents, as == does on Python strings. size() returns the unsigned std::size_t.
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
ZARUSD 6
true
Interview trap: A string literal is a const char[N], not a std::string. Writing "USD" + "EUR" adds two array pointers and does not compile. Wrap one side in std::string first.

Answer: at() checks bounds and throws std::out_of_range. operator[] does not check, so an out-of-range index is undefined behaviour. The exception message text is implementation-specific.
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
4 0.046
caught: vector::_M_range_check: __n (which is 10) >= this->size() (which is 4)
Interview trap: Python's list raises IndexError on any bad index. In C++ the fast path is unchecked, so a bad index may read garbage or corrupt memory without any error.

Answer: push_back may reallocate, which moves every element. References, pointers and iterators into the vector are then invalid. first still refers to the freed buffer.
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
1.13494e-313
The value is leftover heap memory and changes from run to run (three runs gave 1.13494e-313, 1.13833e-313 and 1.14205e-313).
AddressSanitizer output (ASan build): 
==9457==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x502000000010 at pc 0x55ac936d3a7c bp 0x7ffc78c63970 sp 0x7ffc78c63960
    #0 0x55ac936d3a7b in main main.cpp:9
    #1 0x7fb22e62a1c9 in __libc_start_call_main ../sysdeps/nptl/libc_start_call_main.h:58
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free main.cpp:9 in main
Fix: reserve the capacity before taking the reference, or index again after every push_back.
Interview trap: The plain -O2 run printed garbage, not 1. Another build may print the right value, or crash. Undefined behaviour gives no reliable signal, which is why sanitizers are worth running on test code.
reserve(1) then push_back reallocates the buffer, leaving the reference pointing at freed memory.

Answer: std::vector<bool> is a bit-packed specialisation. operator[] returns a proxy object (std::vector<bool>::reference), not a bool&.
g++ diagnostics:
main.cpp:5:23: error: cannot bind non-const lvalue reference of type ‘bool&’ to an rvalue of type ‘bool’
/usr/include/c++/13/bits/stl_bvector.h:99:5: note:   after user-defined conversion: ‘constexpr std::_Bit_reference::operator bool() const’
Fix: use std::vector<char> or std::vector<std::uint8_t> if you need element references, or take the value by copy.
Interview trap: std::vector<bool> is not a container of bool. Generic code that works on vectors of other types may fail to compile with it.

Answer: for (auto x : pv) copies each element into x, so the doubling changes only the copy. auto& aliases the element.
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
100
200
Rule: auto& to modify, const auto& to read without copying an expensive element type.
Interview trap: This is a silent no-op. It compiles, runs and passes a quick look, which makes it easy to miss in review.

front: auto deduction drops {{c1::top-level const and reference}} qualifiers. So with const std::vector<double>& v, the declaration auto x = v; makes x a {{c2::non-const copy}}.
back: Use const auto& x = v; to bind by reference without copying and keep the const. Use auto& if you need to modify through it.

Answer: Objects are destroyed in the reverse order of construction when their scope ends. inner closes at the end of its block. bond and swap close at the end of main, in reverse order.
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
open swap
open bond
open inner
close inner
end of main
close bond
close swap
Python contrast: __del__ timing depends on reference counts and is not something to rely on. C++ destructors run at a known point, which is the basis of RAII (locks, file handles and memory are released by a destructor).
Interview trap: Destructors also run when an exception unwinds the scope, so cleanup done in a destructor is not skipped on error.

Answer: df is an automatic variable that ends when bad_df returns. The reference returned to the caller points to dead storage, and any use is undefined behaviour.
g++ diagnostics:
main.cpp:5:12: warning: reference to local variable ‘df’ returned [-Wreturn-local-addr]
main.cpp:4:12: note: declared here
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
Run exit status: -11 (-11 is SIGSEGV)
AddressSanitizer output (ASan build): 
==9475==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x000000000000 (pc 0x5631c6cc21e5 bp 0x7ffdd4548550 sp 0x7ffdd4548550 T0)
    #0 0x5631c6cc21e5 in std::ostream::operator<<(double) /usr/include/c++/13/ostream:223
    #1 0x5631c6cc21e5 in main main.cpp:9
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: SEGV /usr/include/c++/13/ostream:223 in std::ostream::operator<<(double)
Fix: return by value (double). The function returns a copy, which is cheap for a double and is elided or moved for larger types.
Interview trap: A const T& return is safe only when the referred object outlives the call, such as a data member or a static. Returning a reference to a local is a warning in simple cases, but not in every case.

Answer: enum class is scoped, and its enumerators do not convert implicitly to int.
g++ diagnostics:
main.cpp:4:19: error: cannot convert ‘Side’ to ‘int’ in initialization
Code (fixed version):
#include <iostream>

enum class Side { Buy, Sell };

int main() {
    Side s = Side::Sell;
    std::cout << static_cast<int>(s) << '\n';
    std::cout << (s == Side::Sell) << '\n';
}
Output:
1
1
Interview trap: A plain enum leaks its names into the enclosing scope and converts to int implicitly, which is why enum class is preferred for things like Side.

Answer: C++17. A structured binding unpacks a pair, tuple, array or struct with public members into named variables.
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
1Y 0.04
2Y 0.042
5Y 0.045
3.5
Python contrast: for tenor, rate in curve.items() is the same idea. In C++, const auto& binds to the map entry without copying, and auto& would allow changing rate in the map.
Interview trap: The names refer to parts of a hidden object that the declaration creates (for a by-value auto) or binds to (for auto&). Lifetime follows that object, so a binding to a temporary's part can dangle.

Answer: Reading an uninitialised automatic scalar is undefined behaviour. Its value is indeterminate, and the optimiser may assume any value. The output below is one arbitrary result from this run.
g++ diagnostics:
main.cpp:5:23: warning: ‘n’ is used uninitialized [-Wuninitialized]
main.cpp:4:9: note: ‘n’ was declared here
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
0
Fix: int n{}; (value-initialisation to zero) or int n = 0;.
Interview trap: Class members with no default member initialisers are also indeterminate for built-in types. Python has no equivalent: every name is bound before use or you get a NameError.

Answer: auto y = x; copies the vector, so the Python equivalent is y = list(x). auto& z = x; is an alias, which matches Python's z = x.
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
3 4
4
Interview trap: C++ defaults to value semantics. Reference semantics exist only when you write &, so a copy in a hot loop is an easy performance bug to write.

front: Implement double mean(const std::vector<double>& xs) that throws std::invalid_argument on empty input. Show the code and its test output.
back:
Answer: Take a const& so the vector is not copied. Throw on empty input so an empty series fails at the call site instead of returning NaN or 0.
Code
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <vector>

double mean(const std::vector<double>& xs) {
    if (xs.empty()) throw std::invalid_argument("mean of empty vector");
    double sum = 0.0;
    for (double x : xs) sum += x;
    return sum / static_cast<double>(xs.size());
}

int main() {
    std::cout << mean({1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0}) << '\n';
    try {
        mean({});
    } catch (const std::invalid_argument& e) {
        std::cout << e.what() << '\n';
    }
}
Output (g++ 13.3, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2, run on this machine):
2.5
mean of empty vector
Interview trap: Plain summation accumulates rounding error over long series. For large sums, use compensated (Kahan) summation, or sum pairwise.

front: Build with g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2. -Wall and -Wextra enable {{c1::warnings}}. Add {{c2::-Werror}} to turn warnings into errors so they cannot be ignored. -O2 lets the optimiser exploit {{c3::undefined behaviour}}.
back: Warnings that appeared in this module's snippets: -Wsign-compare, -Wreturn-local-addr and -Wuninitialized (all enabled by -Wall), and -Wimplicit-fallthrough (enabled by -Wextra).
